CausalChain: NAFLD-induced metabolic stress -> Upregulation of FTO in hepatocytes -> Demethylation of m6A sites on mRNAs encoding metabolic enzymes and immune regulators -> Enhanced translation/stability of these transcripts -> Metabolic reprogramming and establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment -> Promotion of liver carcinogenesis
Hypothesis: In NAFLD-associated liver carcinogenesis, metabolic stress triggers FTO upregulation, which in turn demethylates m6A marks on specific metabolic and immune-related mRNAs. This demethylation increases the expression of glycolytic enzymes and immune suppressive factors, thereby driving metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion that collectively promote hepatic tumorigenesis and resistance to therapy.
Abstract: Recent insights into the role of m6A RNA modification in liver carcinogenesis have underscored its complex involvement in gene regulation, metabolic reprogramming, and immune modulation. Building on these findings, we propose that in the context of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), metabolic stress drives the upregulation of the m6A demethylase FTO in hepatocytes. This selective increase in FTO activity leads to the demethylation of key mRNAs that encode glycolytic enzymes and immune regulatory proteins, thereby enhancing their translation and stability. The resultant metabolic shift and creation of an immunosuppressive microenvironment facilitate hepatic tumor initiation, progression, and potentially drug resistance. This hypothesis integrates metabolic stress and m6A-mediated post-transcriptional regulation as dual drivers of liver cancer development and provides a novel framework for targeted therapeutic interventions.
